title: Build until green
about: Every line of code in this film is read from examples/plugged-in, and every line of terminal output is replayed from docs/manual/captures, recorded by running the commands for real.

lines.text: The journeys are agreed, and they're red. Now someone builds.
You don't write a task. You run ortho brief, with the name of one operation: handle.claim.
lines.say: You don't write a task. You run ortho brief, with the name of one operation: handle dot claim.

lines.text: The brief is everything a builder needs, and nothing else. The one file to write. The files to read. What the handler must do.
The paths it must not touch: the blueprint, the journeys, anything generated.
And what done means: prove passes, and check passes. Hand it over exactly as printed.
The builder doesn't start from an empty file. Generate has already written a scaffold: the frame, with a blank where the behaviour goes.
First run. It proves only the one journey: claim a handle.
Four of eight steps pass before a line is written. Those are the steps that never needed this handler.
And the first failure names the blank the handler reached, and the file it's in. That's where the builder goes.
So it writes the work. Two records, saved together: the handle, and its public page.
Prove again. Still four of eight.
The number didn't move. But read the reasons. Before: the server died. Now: answered, without making its move.
The handler saved the records and forgot to change the state. So there's no event, and no state. The failure says exactly that.
This is what climbing looks like. Not every rung turns a light green. But every rung changes what fails first.
One line: make the move.
Prove again. Eight of eight.
But look at the last line. Prove is still red, with five failing. One journey doesn't reach every operation, so coverage fails.
Green on one journey is not done. The builder runs the whole proof.
Seven journeys. Fifty-six steps. Nine evals for each of seven operations. Prove passes. Then check passes.
You read none of that code. You read one line for each journey, and the last line of the full run.
When a builder says a journey is wrong, it stops, and tells the author. It doesn't edit the story, and it doesn't work round it.
When a handler starts deciding things the blueprint never said, that's a finding for review.
One honest note. What you just watched is a replay. We put one handler at three points, and recorded the real run at each. No agent was filmed writing it.
The loop is real, and an agent can run it alone. Next: run the app, break it, and read the trace.
